summary: Defines a MIB for monitoring X.500 Directory System Agents, to be used together with the Application MIB. It was replaced by RFC 2605.

eli5.summary: A set of gauges to check on directory servers, such as how busy they are.

subtitle: Monitoring X.500 directory servers with SNMP operations and cache metrics

tldr.problem: Directory system administrators need to monitor X.500 directory servers to track lookup requests, security events, and how well the cache is performing.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1567 defines three MIB tables: one for operations counters (binds, reads, searches, errors), one for entry statistics and cache performance, and one for tracking interactions with peer directory servers.
tldr.outcome: Operators can use SNMP to query live operation counts and cache hit rates from their directory servers. The MIB was later superseded by RFC 2605.

facts.label: DSA operations
facts.value: Read, Compare, AddEntry, ModifyEntry, ModifyRDN, RemoveEntry, List, Search

today: RFC 1567 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 2605.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1567 defines a Management Information Base (MIB) for monitoring Directory System Agents (DSAs), which are the servers in the X.500 Directory. The X.500 Directory is a global hierarchical directory service defined by CCITT that stores information about people, organizations, and resources on the Internet and in OSI networks.

A DSA responds to lookup requests from directory user agents (clients) and other DSAs, and it may forward requests to other DSAs to complete them. The MIB provides standardized SNMP objects to monitor how the DSA is being used and how well it is performing, including operation counts, cache efficiency, and communication success with peer servers.
sections.eli5: A DSA is a server that answers questions like "Where is this person?" or "What is this company's address?" This MIB counts how many questions it gets, how many work, and whether its memory cache is helping.

sections.title: DSA Components and Data Model
sections.content:
A DSA's local database consists of three categories of entries. Master entries are the authoritative copy of the data. Copy entries are slave replications (shadow copies) kept for availability. Cache entries are non-authoritative copies retrieved from elsewhere and stored temporarily to speed up future lookups. Cache can significantly improve performance because many lookups are repeated.

The DSA performs eight types of operations: Read, Compare, AddEntry, ModifyEntry, ModifyRDN (rename), RemoveEntry, List, and Search. Clients can authenticate using anonymous access, unauthenticated access, simple authentication (a password), or strong authentication (digital signatures). The MIB tracks all of these categories separately.
sections.eli5: The directory server has three kinds of stored data: the official copy it owns, backup copies, and temporary saved answers. It handles eight kinds of requests, and tracks whether people asking the questions logged in or not.

sections.title: Operations Table
sections.content:
The dsaOpsTable provides counters for all types of DSA activity. It tracks binds by authentication type: dsaAnonymousBinds, dsaUnauthBinds, dsaSimpleAuthBinds, and dsaStrongAuthBinds, as well as dsaBindSecurityErrors for failed authentications.

For operations, it counts dsaReadOps, dsaCompareOps, dsaAddEntryOps, dsaRemoveEntryOps, dsaModifyEntryOps, dsaModifyRDNOps, dsaListOps, and dsaSearchOps (split into dsaOneLevelSearchOps and dsaWholeTreeSearchOps). It also tracks dsaReferrals (when the DSA tells a client to ask another DSA) and dsaChainings (when the DSA forwards the request to another DSA on behalf of the client). Finally, it counts dsaSecurityErrors and dsaErrors for failed operations.
sections.eli5: The server counts how many people asked for things and what they asked for. It counts successful answers, referrals to other servers, and different kinds of errors.

sections.title: Entry Statistics and Cache Performance
sections.content:
The dsaEntriesTable provides a snapshot of the DSA's data and cache health. dsaMasterEntries and dsaCopyEntries are gauges showing how many entries are currently stored. dsaCacheEntries shows temporary cached entries.

dsaCacheHits and dsaSlaveHits are counters showing how often operations were answered from the cache or from slave copies, respectively, since startup. A high cache-hit rate means the DSA is efficiently reusing stored data. A low hit rate might indicate the cache size is too small or that lookups are very diverse.
sections.eli5: These are dials showing how much data is stored and how often the saved copy of data was useful instead of having to look it up fresh.

sections.title: Peer DSA Interactions
sections.content:
The dsaIntTable tracks the monitored DSA's interactions with peer DSAs. Each row represents one peer and records when the entry was created, when the last connection attempt was made, when the last successful connection happened, and how many failures have occurred since the last success.

The dsaName field stores the Distinguished Name of the peer DSA. Counters include total failures and successes, plus dsaFailuresSinceLastSuccess, which helps identify chronically problematic peers. This table helps administrators spot which distant DSAs are hard to reach or unreliable.
sections.eli5: This tracks each server on the network that this DSA talks to, and whether it can reach them. If one is always broken, the admin knows there is a problem to fix.
